message.content:
City Council Approves Major Transit Overhaul to Ease Downtown Congestion

By Elena Martinez
City Desk

April 14, 2026

The City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to approve a sweeping transit overhaul aimed at easing chronic traffic congestion and improving access to jobs and services across the metropolitan area. The plan — the most significant transportation investment in the city’s history — includes expanded bus rapid transit (BRT), new protected bike lanes, and the creation of a congestion pricing zone in the downtown core.

Mayor David Chen hailed the plan as a turning point. “Today we chose to invest in a city that moves — more equitably, more sustainably, and smarter,” Chen said after the vote. “These changes won’t just speed commutes; they’ll expand opportunity for families throughout our neighborhoods.”

Key elements of the plan

- Bus Rapid Transit: Eight new BRT corridors will be built or upgraded over the next five years, creating high-frequency, limited-stop service that officials say could cut transit travel times by up to 30 percent on major routes. Dedicated lanes, signal prioritization, and improved stations are included.

- Congestion pricing: Vehicles entering the central business district during weekday peak hours will face a fee, with exemptions for emergency vehicles and certain small businesses. Revenue generated will be ring-fenced for transit improvements and reduced fares for low-income riders.

- Active transportation: The city will add 45 miles of protected bike lanes and dozens of pedestrian safety upgrades, including safer crossings and curb extensions at high-injury intersections.

- Fleet electrification and accessibility: The municipal bus fleet will begin transitioning to zero-emission vehicles, and all new stations and vehicles will meet enhanced accessibility standards.

Public reaction

Supporters celebrated the vote as overdue action to tackle worsening congestion and climate targets. “This is the kind of leadership our city needs,” said Rosa Patel, director of the nonprofit Transit for All. “Faster buses and safer streets will make it easier for people without cars to get to work and school.”

But some small business owners and commuters pushed back. At a town hall earlier this month, restaurant owner Miguel Alvarez warned that congestion fees could hurt delivery-dependent businesses. “We already operate on thin margins,” Alvarez said. “Additional costs could be the difference between staying open and shutting our doors.”

Council members say the plan includes measures to soften the impact on small businesses, such as discounted fees during the first year and subsidies for delivery micro-hubs located just outside the congestion zone.

Funding and timeline

The plan’s estimated price tag is $1.8 billion. Funding will come from a mix of municipal bonds, state and federal grants, and congestion pricing revenue. Officials estimate the first construction phase will begin in late 2026, with key BRT corridors and initial bike lanes completed by 2029.

Transportation Director Leila Hassan emphasized that careful staging and community engagement will guide implementation. “We’ll pilot corridor changes, solicit feedback, and adjust before making permanent street redesigns,” Hassan said. “The goal is to minimize disruption while delivering tangible benefits quickly.”

Equity and climate goals

City officials framed the overhaul as integral to the city’s climate plan, projecting a 15 percent reduction in transportation emissions by 2035 if modal shifts from single-occupancy vehicles to transit, walking, and cycling meet targets. The plan also includes a low-income transit pass program to ensure affordability and equitable access.

Neighborhood advocates say they will monitor outcomes closely. “We want to see concrete commitments on fare equity and service to historically underserved neighborhoods,” said Marcus Reed, president of the Eastside Neighborhood Coalition. “Promises are good, but delivery matters.”

What’s next

The council’s vote clears the way for detailed design work and procurement. A series of community workshops and public hearings are scheduled over the coming months to refine corridor alignments, station locations, and the structure of the congestion fee.

Transportation planners estimate that, if implemented as designed, the overhaul could significantly reduce peak-hour traffic downtown while improving reliability for the city’s bus network — a lifeline for many residents who depend on it for daily travel.

“We have the opportunity to reshape how our city moves,” Mayor Chen said. “If we do this right, we’ll create a cleaner, fairer, more connected city for generations to come.”
